strengths: Novel force decomposition perspective: The analysis of optimization trajectory drift through pushing/pulling forces and parallel/perpendicular components provides fresh insights into contrastive learning optimization dynamics
Rigorous mathematical analysis: Clear gradient derivations in Section 2 and Appendix C showing how SVR scales the perpendicular component by factor (1 - R/||a⁺ - t⁺||)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough ablation studies across monolingual/multilingual settings, zero-shot classification, different batch sizes, SVR weights, with analysis of overhead and radius evolution
Consistent improvements across tasks: Demonstrates gains over InfoNCE baseline on AudioCaps (R@1: 41.87→44.16), Clotho (R@1: 18.67→19.75), and classification benchmarks
Practical efficiency: Negligible computational overhead (Table 9) enables easy integration into existing frameworks
Well-presented with clear visualizations: Effective use of figures to illustrate global/local perpendicular components and drift measurement, detailed appendices enhance reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification: The connection between reducing the perpendicular component and improved alignment is not rigorously established—why should suppressing this 'double-edged sword' component (which carries valuable discriminative information) improve performance? No convergence analysis provided

Figure 1 contradicts core narrative: Drift increases in later training stages, which the authors dismiss as 'expected' behavior. This undermines the claim that trajectory drift is inherently problematic. The paper doesn't clearly establish what cost drift actually imposes on final performance

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against InfoNCE and SigLIP (2023). Missing head-to-head comparisons with recent strong methods cited in related work (Yuan et al. 2024 T-CLAP, Ghosh et al. 2025 RECLAP, Xie et al. 2024 GPA) under controlled conditions
Modest empirical improvements: Typical gains of 2-3 R@1 points (~5-7% relative) without statistical significance testing, making it unclear if improvements are meaningful or within noise

Unjustified design choices: (1) Why displace text toward audio rather than other geometric constructions? No ablation provided. (2) Constraint term (Appendix B) with Lcons and β=0.01 appears ad-hoc. (3) Bidirectional SVR works better but analysis focuses on unidirectional—why? (4) No intuitive justification for why similarity vector S should predict semantic radius R

Limited scope and scale: Single GPU, 10 epochs only; datasets are small (AudioCaps ~49k, Clotho ~7k); only audio-text tested; generalization to other modalities unknown; using non-state-of-the-art encoders (CED-Base, SONAR-TE)

Imprecise terminology and missing analyses: Terms like 'trajectory drift' and 'pushing/pulling forces' are metaphorical rather than formally defined. Missing: (1) visualization of learned embeddings, (2) error analysis or failure cases, (3) interpretation of radius variation semantics, (4) analysis of which audio-text pairs benefit most

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned; multilingual results rely on LLM translation with quality assessed only via back-translation similarity; unclear hyperparameter tuning parity across methods

strengths: Novel problem formulation identifying and formalizing optimization trajectory drift in contrastive learning through force decomposition—a perspective not previously highlighted in audio-text pretraining literature
Rigorous mathematical analysis with clear derivations showing how SVR suppresses the perpendicular component via factor (1 - R/||a+ - t+||); theory is well-supported by experiments (Figures 1-3)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (AudioCaps, Clotho), scenarios (monolingual, multilingual, zero-shot), and ablation studies covering directional variants, batch sizes, and hyperparameters
Practical efficiency with negligible computational overhead (<2% in Table 9), making the method immediately deployable in existing CLAP pipelines

Consistent empirical improvements across all tasks (5-6% relative gains; e.g., 44.16 vs 41.87 on AudioCaps T2A R@1) with well-motivated design choices including principled constraint terms for DynamicSVR
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core SVR mechanism is straightforward (adding an auxiliary contrastive loss with displaced support vectors). The 'Support Vector' naming is somewhat misleading as it doesn't leverage SVM principles, and related work (T-MASS, Max-Margin Contrastive Learning) already explored auxiliary vector constraints, though with different motivation

Informal theoretical framework: 'trajectory drift' is defined operationally (cosine similarity to pulling force) without justifying why this specific metric is the right choice. The paper demonstrates SVR suppresses the perpendicular component empirically but doesn't rigorously prove optimality—more empirical than theoretical

Severely limited baseline comparisons: only InfoNCE and SigLIP compared in main results. Recent strong CLAP methods (T-CLAP, Cacophony, COMPA, DSCLAP) cited in related work are absent from Tables 1-2. Unclear whether improvements come from the SVR insight or simply adding regularization

Semantic radius modeling lacks principled foundation: why the similarity vector S is sufficient to predict optimal R is never justified theoretically. The constraint term (Relu(R - ||a+ - t+||) + Relu(-R)) appears ad-hoc rather than principled. Only modest ablation on constraint weight β (set to 0.01)

Experimental setup limitations: small datasets (AudioCaps ~49k, Clotho ~7k by modern standards), short training (10 epochs), small batch size (24), multilingual setup relies on LLM translations validated only via back-translation with single metric (~90% RoBERTa similarity). No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple runs reported. Modest absolute improvements in some cases (1-2% absolute on Clotho) raise questions about statistical significance

strengths: Clear identification and geometric analysis of optimization trajectory drift in contrastive learning, with intuitive force decomposition framework and good visualization (Figure 2)

Rigorous mathematical analysis including gradient decomposition (Section 2.1), convergence speed proof showing perpendicular component as noise penalty (Appendix C), and SVR mechanism analysis (Appendix D)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (AudioCaps, Clotho, WavCaps), monolingual/multilingual/zero-shot settings, 5-run statistical significance testing, extensive ablations, convergence analysis, and robustness studies
Consistent improvements across InfoNCE and SigLIP baselines on diverse benchmarks, with practical efficiency (negligible computational overhead, no extra training data)
Thoughtful design including constraint term to address DynamicSVR failure modes, bidirectional application strategy, and robustness to noisy embeddings
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is identifying perpendicular gradient components slow convergence and adding a regularization term—this is incremental relative to existing gradient control and variance reduction techniques; misleading 'Support Vector' naming unrelated to classical SVMs

Incomplete theoretical justification: proves F⊥ slows convergence to specific positive pair (Eq. 12) but doesn't rigorously establish this improves final alignment quality or generalization; circular reasoning on whether suppressing F⊥ is universally beneficial

Ad-hoc semantic radius modeling: StaticSVR assumes global radius works uniformly; DynamicSVR uses unsupervised MLP training without explicit objective, with constraint term appearing as a patch rather than principled design; qualitative explanation of radius decay over time (Figure 3)
Modest practical improvements: ~1-2% absolute gains on several datasets (Clotho: 18.67%→19.75%, AudioCaps: 41.87%→44.16% R@1); unclear if improvements are due to encoders or SVR specifically
Narrow scope and generalization concerns: specific to audio-text CLAP with normalized embeddings; no evidence transfer to vision-language or other domains; requires bidirectional application

Missing comparative baselines: no comparison with gradient clipping, variance reduction methods, or other contrastive learning improvements; Simple Reweight baseline limited; ATRI integration claims orthogonality without deep investigation

Incomplete causal analysis: connection between Figure 1's drift metric and final performance is correlational; no analysis of potential negative effects (robustness, OOD generalization); hard negatives study (E.8) only examines density
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; LLM-translated multilingual test sets may not be easily reproducible; minimal predictor architecture documentation

strengths: Clear geometric intuition: The decomposition of gradients into pulling/pushing forces with analysis of perpendicular components provides an accessible perspective on optimization dynamics, well illustrated in Figures 1-2.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: Sound mathematical derivations showing perpendicular component as 'noise penalty' (Eq. 12) and detailed SVR mechanism analysis (Appendix D) with correct scaling factor derivation.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation on multiple datasets (AudioCaps, Clotho, WavCaps, ESC-50, US8K), diverse settings (monolingual/multilingual, zero-shot), statistical significance testing (5 runs with confidence intervals), and extensive ablations.
Practical efficiency: Method adds negligible computational overhead (~1-2% training time) while improving performance, with consistent 2-4% gains in R@1 across datasets.

Methodological rigor: Simple Reweight baseline comparison (Table 7) demonstrates improvements are from geometric effects, not just gradient rescaling. Robustness analysis covers noisy settings, hard negatives, and distribution shift.
Convergence validation: Figure 5 empirically supports theoretical analysis by showing faster convergence with SVR-enhanced models across multiple configurations.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core observation: Gradient deviation from positive pair direction is well-established in contrastive learning literature. Paper lacks adequate positioning relative to gradient-aware methods and overstates the 'double-edged sword' characterization of perpendicular components.

Insufficient justification for SVR design: Why displace support vectors along the pulling direction (t⁺ - a⁺) specifically? Why is tsup = t⁺ + Rû optimal? Alternative constructions are unexplored. Paper doesn't prove SVR is optimal for drift control, only that it works empirically.

Misleading 'semantic radius' terminology: The mechanism is purely geometric, not semantic. Limited interpretation of why R should correlate with embedding geometry or be instance-specific. Figure 3 shows R decreases during training but lacks clear mechanistic explanation.

DynamicSVR design appears ad-hoc: Constraint term Lcons (Eq. 9) uses soft ReLU penalties rather than principled design. The need for constraints suggests the predictor learns an unconstrained problem. Marginal benefit over StaticSVR (<1% in some cases, within confidence intervals).

Incomplete related work positioning: Limited differentiation from hard negative mining and gradient regularization techniques. Only Simple Reweight baseline tested; no comparison with other gradient-aware contrastive methods or trajectory stabilization approaches.

Drift measurement concerns: Figure 1 shows baseline InfoNCE drift increasing over epochs—counterintuitive and unexplained. Cosine similarity between update vector and pulling force is reasonable but not validated as optimal metric.

Experimental setup limitations: Only 10 training epochs; primary batch size 24 with limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. Results may be configuration-specific. Multilingual results relegated to appendix with translation quality variation (90-95%).
Modest improvement magnitude: Consistent but small gains (2-4% R@1); marginal benefit of complex DynamicSVR over simple StaticSVR raises questions about practical significance for practitioners.
